# Exact real-fiber interpolation in one integer coordinate

Let `d>=1` and let the actual nonempty integer fibers of a convex body
be compact convex sets `K_j subset R^d`, `j=a,...,b`. The fibers may
have different affine dimensions, including dimension zero. Replace the
original body by

    C_*=conv union_(j=a)^b ({j} x K_j).

This replacement preserves every integer fiber: convexity of the
original body gives one inclusion and the displayed union gives the
other. Let

    D_int=conv union_j(K_j-K_j),
    D_all(C_*)={v:(0,v) in C_*-C_*}.

Then, in every continuous dimension,

    (C_*)_(j+t)=(1-t)K_j+t K_(j+1),  0<=t<=1,             (1)
    D_all(C_*)=D_int.                                      (2)

These are exact equalities; no limit, lattice-width assumption, or
selection of a mixed-integer center is involved.

## Proof

Fix a continuous covector u. Actual convex compatibility implies the
sequence `f_u(j)=h_Kj(u)` is concave: for any integer j between integers
i,k, the fiber K_j contains the corresponding Minkowski interpolation
of K_i and K_k. Its support in direction u is therefore at least the
same interpolation of their supports.

The continuous function F_u that linearly interpolates f_u on each
adjacent unit interval is concave. Indeed its successive slopes are
nonincreasing by discrete concavity. Hence for any probability weights
lambda_i of real mean `s in [a,b]`,

    sum_i lambda_i f_u(i)<=F_u(s).

Every point of the real fiber `(C_*)_s` is a convex combination of
points of the integer fibers with those same base-coordinate weights.
Its u-coordinate is at most F_u(s). On the other hand the adjacent
Minkowski interpolation at s belongs to `(C_*)_s`, and its support is
exactly F_u(s). These two bounds give equality of the support functions
in every u, proving (1) for compact convex sets. No volume or interior
assumption entered this support-function argument.

The directional width of the fiber in (1) is

    (1-t)[h_Kj(u)+h_Kj(-u)]
      +t[h_K(j+1)(u)+h_K(j+1)(-u)].

It is bounded by the largest integer-fiber width in this direction,
and that width is attained by an integer fiber. The union of all real
fiber differences is exactly `{v:(0,v) in C_*-C_*}`, which is already
convex. Its support function is the maximum of those real-fiber
widths. This proves (2). The case a=b is immediate from one fiber.
QED.

## Why the replacement by conv(S) is essential

For example take the convex hull of `[0,1] x [-1/2,1/2]` and the two
points `(1/2,+L),(1/2,-L)`, with `L>=1/2`. Its only integer fibers are
the two unit intervals. Thus D_int is `[-1,1]`, while the original
D_all contains `[-2L,2L]`. The convex hull of the integer fibers alone
is the original unit rectangle and obeys (2). Real bulges between
integer fibers cannot be retained in that identity.

## Related comparison from a common affine section

For an arbitrary finite actual base P, suppose there is an affine map
`c:aff(P)->R^d` with `c(z) in K_z` at every integer index. Then

    D_int subset D_all(C_*) subset 2 D_int.                 (3)

Extend c affinely to R^n and use the legitimate fiber shear
`x->x-c(z)`. Each integer fiber
contains zero and is therefore contained in its own difference body,
hence in D_int. Every real fiber of their convex hull is contained in
D_int as well. Taking two points in such a fiber proves the second
inclusion in (3); the first is immediate. Both difference bodies are
unchanged by that shear.

The factor two is exact under this hypothesis. On the binary square
take interval fibers `[-1,0]` at `(0,0),(1,1)` and `[0,1]` at
`(0,1),(1,0)`. The common affine section is zero, and D_int is
`[-1,1]`. At the real midpoint `(1/2,1/2)`, the opposite diagonal
mixtures give the full interval `[-1,1]`, so D_all is `[-2,2]`.

Such a common affine section always exists when conv(P) is a simplex:
choose one point in each vertex fiber and affinely interpolate those
points. Compatibility puts the interpolated point in every K_z.
The comparison (3) then applies. It does not assert equality in
higher integer dimension.

## Comparison from an integer core with explicit radial asymmetry

More generally, let `z0 in P` lie in the relative interior of conv(P).
Let R>0 be any finite constant such that

    conv(P)-z0 subset R[z0-conv(P)].

Then, for the convex hull C_* of the actual fibers,

    D_all(C_*) subset (1+R)(K_z0-K_z0)
                   subset (1+R)D_int.                     (4)

For every real p in conv(P), the point
`q=z0-(p-z0)/R` belongs to conv(P), and
`z0=(p+Rq)/(1+R)`. Fix one point in the nonempty real fiber at q.
Convexity puts a translate of `(1/(1+R))(C_*)_p` in K_z0.
Taking differences gives (4) for every real p, and then for their
union. This is a quantitative comparison with the stated geometric
parameter R, not a dimension-only bound on arbitrary integer cores.

## Exact limitation of capwise trace-preserving clipping

Equality (2) does not itself bound the hinge of a fixed cap trace.
Take `P={-N,...,N}` with integer `N>=1` and identical interval fibers
`K_j=[-1/2,1/2]`. Then `D_int=D_all=[-1,1]` and `M=2N+1`.
The cap `z+x>=0` has the upper half of the central interval, every
positive-index interval, and none of the negative-index intervals.

Any affine cap with the same trace on S, represented with continuous
normal of absolute value one, must have margin

    x+A z,  A>=1/2.

The continuous normal and zero offset are forced by the proper
central half-interval. Inclusion of the entire fiber at z=1 forces
`A>=1/2`; exact exclusion at z=-1 actually makes this inequality
strict if the trace is required pointwise, which only strengthens
the lower bound below. Its hinge is therefore at least

    1/8 + (1/2) sum_(j=1)^N j
      =1/8+N(N+1)/4.                                     (5)

Its cap mass is always `N+1/2=M/2`, but (5) divided by M tends to
infinity. Thus a uniform compression cannot be performed by merely
clipping affine coefficients while preserving every cap trace.
Changing or discarding caps is necessary. This is only a limitation
of that capwise operation: the horizontal pair `x>=0,-x>=0` already
gives the same M/2 budget and hinge bounded relative to M for this whole body.
No full-cardinality compression obstruction is claimed here.
